subject: physics

items.q: A circuit diagram shows a component drawn as a plain rectangle with an arrow across it at an angle. Which component is it?
items.correct: a variable resistor, whose resistance is set by hand by moving a slider
items.misconception: an LDR, whose resistance falls when the light shining on it brightens
items.why: Several symbols are built on the resistor rectangle, so students group them by meaning rather than by the marking that actually distinguishes them. The arrow across the rectangle means the resistance can be set by hand. A thermistor has a line bent at right angles; an LDR is a rectangle inside a circle with arrows pointing in at it.
items.random_wrong: a thermistor, whose resistance changes when its temperature alters

items.q: A student is drawing a circuit diagram to measure the current through a lamp and the potential difference across it. Where should the two meters be drawn?
items.correct: the ammeter in the loop with the lamp and the voltmeter across it
items.misconception: the voltmeter in the loop with the lamp, and the ammeter across it
items.why: Both are meters that look alike on a diagram, and students remember that one goes in and one goes across without a reason to attach to each. Nothing in the two names tells them which is which. A voltmeter compares the potential at the two ends of a component, so it must be connected to both ends — across it. An ammeter counts the charge passing through, so the charge must go through it — in the loop.
items.random_wrong: both meters drawn in the loop, one on each side of the lamp

items.q: A closed loop of copper wire contains no cell and no power supply. Why is there no current in it?
items.correct: there is no source of potential difference to make the charge flow
items.misconception: the free electrons in the copper drift round on their own, making a current
items.why: The rule most often repeated is that the circuit must be complete, and students take that necessary condition to be sufficient on its own. The free electrons are indeed already there, but they move at random in all directions. A source of pd is needed to give them a net drift in one direction, which is what a current is.
items.random_wrong: a complete copper loop needs no cell, so a current flows round it

items.q: What is meant by the size of the electric current in a wire?
items.correct: the rate of flow of electrical charge past a given point in the wire
items.misconception: the total charge that has flowed since the circuit was switched on
items.why: Both words appear in the same definition sentence, and both are met through the same equipment, so the distinction between an amount and a rate is lost. The coulomb is an amount of charge, like a distance; the ampere is a rate, like a speed. One ampere is one coulomb passing each second, which is why Q = I t.
items.random_wrong: the speed at which the individual electrons drift along the wire

items.q: A current of 0.40 A passes through a lamp for 5.0 minutes. Calculate the charge flow.
items.why: The equation is memorised as V = I R, a multiplication, and the multiplication sign is then carried over into every rearrangement of it. Rearranging V = I R gives R = V ÷ I and I = V ÷ R. Only the subject of the original equation is a product; the other two are quotients.

items.q: In the equation Q = I t, which set of units is correct for the three quantities?
items.correct: charge flow in coulombs, current in amperes, time in seconds
items.misconception: charge flow in amperes, current in coulombs, and time in seconds
items.why: Both words appear in the same definition sentence, and both are met through the same equipment, so the distinction between an amount and a rate is lost. The coulomb is an amount of charge, like a distance; the ampere is a rate, like a speed. One ampere is one coulomb passing each second, which is why Q = I t.
items.random_wrong: charge flow in coulombs, current in amperes and time in minutes

items.q: Two identical lamps are in series with a cell. An ammeter between the cell and the first lamp reads 0.30 A. It is then moved to a position between the two lamps. What does it read now?
items.correct: 0.30 A, because a current has the same value everywhere in one loop
items.misconception: less than 0.30 A, because the first lamp has used up some current
items.why: Students can see the lamps glowing and know that something is being used up, and the everyday word current suggests a supply that runs out. The energy transferred by the lamps is real, so the loss is wrongly pinned on the current. What the lamps use is energy, not charge. Every coulomb that leaves the cell passes through both lamps and returns to it, so the current is identical at every point in the loop.
items.random_wrong: less than 0.30 A, because the meter is now further from the cell

items.q: A resistor in a circuit is replaced by one of greater resistance, and the potential difference across it is unchanged. What happens to the current through it?
items.correct: it decreases, because a greater resistance opposes the flow of charge
items.misconception: it stays the same, because the cell always pushes out the same current
items.why: Cells are labelled with a fixed number of volts, and students transfer that fixedness to the current, treating the cell as a pump that delivers a set amount whatever it is connected to. The number on a cell is its potential difference, not its current. The current is decided by the pd and the resistance together: I = V ÷ R.
items.random_wrong: it stays the same, because the pd across the component is unchanged

items.q: A potential difference of 6.0 V across a component produces a current of 0.25 A through it. Calculate the resistance of the component.
items.why: The equation is memorised as V = I R, a multiplication, and the multiplication sign is then carried over into every rearrangement of it. Rearranging V = I R gives R = V ÷ I and I = V ÷ R. Only the subject of the original equation is a product; the other two are quotients.

items.q: A resistor of resistance 15 Ω has a potential difference of 3.0 V across it. Calculate the current through the resistor.
items.why: The equation is memorised as V = I R, a multiplication, and the multiplication sign is then carried over into every rearrangement of it. Rearranging V = I R gives R = V ÷ I and I = V ÷ R. Only the subject of the original equation is a product; the other two are quotients.

items.q: In Required practical activity 3 a student doubles the length of nichrome wire in the circuit while keeping its temperature constant. What happens to the resistance of the wire?
items.correct: it doubles, because resistance is proportional to the wire length
items.misconception: it halves, because a longer wire gives the charge more room to move in
items.why: Length is confused with thickness. Students correctly know that a wider wire has less resistance, and more room sounds like the same idea. A longer wire means more metal for the charge to push through, so more collisions and more resistance. It is a wider cross-section, not a greater length, that lowers resistance.
items.random_wrong: it is unchanged, since resistance depends only on the metal in use

items.q: A second resistor, identical to the first, is connected in parallel with it. What happens to the total resistance of the combination?
items.correct: it halves, because the charge now has two separate paths to flow along
items.misconception: it doubles, because two resistors must resist more than one of them
items.why: The series case is met first and then generalised. The word resistor sounds like something that can only ever add opposition to the circuit. In series the charge must pass through both, so the resistances add. In parallel the charge divides between two paths, so the combined resistance is smaller than either resistor on its own.
items.random_wrong: it stays the same, since both resistors have the same resistance

items.q: In Required practical activity 3 a student wants to find the resistance of a length of wire. Which pair of measurements is needed?
items.correct: the pd across the wire and the current in it
items.misconception: readings from a voltmeter in the loop and an ammeter
items.why: Both are meters that look alike on a diagram, and students remember that one goes in and one goes across without a reason to attach to each. Nothing in the two names tells them which is which. A voltmeter compares the potential at the two ends of a component, so it must be connected to both ends — across it. An ammeter counts the charge passing through, so the charge must go through it — in the loop.
items.random_wrong: the pd across the wire and the charge that flows in it

items.q: In the resistance practical, why is the voltmeter connected across the test wire rather than in the loop with it?
items.correct: because it must compare the potentials at the two ends of the wire
items.misconception: because a voltmeter in the loop would read the current in it instead
items.why: Reverse is attached to the meters, the most obviously reversible things on the bench, rather than to the direction of the pd across the component. Reversing means reversing the direction of the pd across the component. Swapping the meters would simply produce a wrong circuit, with the ammeter shorting out the component.
items.random_wrong: because a voltmeter, like the ammeter, belongs in the loop

items.q: Which statement about the resistance of circuit components is correct?
items.correct: for some components R is constant, in others it changes with current
items.misconception: R is a fixed property of every component, in the way that mass is fixed
items.why: Resistance is first met as a value printed on a resistor, and printed values feel permanent. Fixed resistor is often shortened to resistor, which hides the distinction. Resistance is fixed only for an ohmic conductor at constant temperature. For lamps, diodes, thermistors and LDRs it changes with the current, and with temperature or light level.
items.random_wrong: R never changes, not even in a thermistor or an LDR

items.q: The I–V graph for a resistor at constant temperature is a straight line passing through the origin. What does this show?
items.correct: the current is directly proportional to the pd, so the resistance is constant
items.misconception: the resistance rises steadily as the potential difference is increased
items.why: The rule met first is the metal wire one — hot filament, higher resistance — and it is generalised to every component. The thermistor is the exception, and exceptions are easily overwritten. A thermistor is a semiconductor, not a metal. Heating it frees more charge carriers, so its resistance drops. That opposite behaviour is exactly what makes it useful as a temperature sensor.
items.random_wrong: the resistance is equal to the gradient of the line at every point

items.q: As the current through a filament lamp increases, what happens to the resistance of the lamp, and why?
items.correct: it increases, because the filament becomes hotter
items.misconception: it stays constant, because the lamp is an ohmic conductor
items.why: Students take through the origin as the whole test and stop there, or they take rising together to mean directly proportional. A curve that rises does look like agreement with the rule. Directly proportional means a straight line through the origin, so that equal increases in pd give equal increases in current. The lamp's line bends over, so its resistance is not constant.
items.random_wrong: it stays constant, because its I–V graph passes through the origin

items.q: A diode is connected into a circuit the reverse way round. What is the current through it?
items.correct: almost zero, because the diode has a very high resistance in reverse
items.misconception: a tiny current, because the diode still leaks a little in reverse
items.why: Diodes are described as one-way, which students soften into mostly one way, and the forward direction is then imagined as a perfectly free path. In reverse the resistance is so high that the current is effectively zero. In the forward direction the diode does have resistance, and needs a pd of a few tenths of a volt before it conducts at all.
items.random_wrong: much smaller than the forward current, but still easy to measure

items.q: A thermistor is taken out of a beaker of iced water and placed in a beaker of hot water. What happens to its resistance?
items.correct: it decreases, since a thermistor's resistance falls as it warms
items.misconception: it increases, because heating any conductor raises its resistance
items.why: The rule met first is the metal wire one — hot filament, higher resistance — and it is generalised to every component. The thermistor is the exception, and exceptions are easily overwritten. A thermistor is a semiconductor, not a metal. Heating it frees more charge carriers, so its resistance drops. That opposite behaviour is exactly what makes it useful as a temperature sensor.
items.random_wrong: it stays the same, because resistance depends on the material only

items.q: A thermistor is used in a thermostat that switches a heater on when a room becomes too cold. What happens in the circuit as the room cools?
items.correct: the thermistor's resistance rises, and the circuit then switches the heater on
items.misconception: the thermistor's resistance falls, letting a larger current switch it on
items.why: Students reason backwards from the outcome: the heater comes on, so something must increase, and a bigger current feels like the obvious cause. Cold means high resistance for a thermistor, since its resistance falls as temperature rises. It is that rise in resistance, detected as a change in pd across the thermistor, that the switching circuit responds to.
items.random_wrong: the thermistor's resistance falls, so the heater stays switched off

items.q: The light shining on an LDR is made brighter. What happens to the resistance of the LDR?
items.correct: it decreases as the light on it gets brighter
items.misconception: it increases, as there is more light for it to resist
items.why: The name light-dependent resistor is read as light causes resistance, and more of a cause is expected to give more of an effect. Light energy frees charge carriers inside the LDR, so more light makes it a better conductor, not a worse one. In darkness its resistance is highest, often millions of ohms.
items.random_wrong: it stays constant whatever the light level may be

items.q: An LDR is part of a circuit that switches a street lamp on when it gets dark. What happens as darkness falls?
items.correct: the LDR's resistance rises, and so the circuit switches the lamp on
items.misconception: the LDR's resistance falls, so a bigger current can switch the lamp on
items.why: The same backwards reasoning as with the thermostat: the lamp switching on is associated with something increasing, so a falling resistance and a rising current are assumed. Darkness means less light, so the LDR's resistance is high, not low. The switching circuit reacts to that high resistance and to the pd it produces.
items.random_wrong: the LDR's resistance falls, so the lamp is kept switched off

items.q: Which circuit would let a student measure the resistance of a fixed resistor?
items.correct: an ammeter in the loop and a voltmeter across the resistor
items.misconception: a voltmeter in the loop with an ammeter across the resistor
items.why: Both are meters that look alike on a diagram, and students remember that one goes in and one goes across without a reason to attach to each. Nothing in the two names tells them which is which. A voltmeter compares the potential at the two ends of a component, so it must be connected to both ends — across it. An ammeter counts the charge passing through, so the charge must go through it — in the loop.
items.random_wrong: an ammeter and a voltmeter both in the loop with the resistor

items.q: A student plots I–V graphs for a fixed resistor at constant temperature and for a filament lamp. What do the two shapes tell her?
items.correct: the resistor is a linear element of constant R, while the lamp is non-linear and its R rises
items.misconception: the resistor has the greater resistance, because its line is the steeper
items.why: Steeper is read as more of whatever the graph is about, and students do not check which quantity is on which axis before deciding. On I–V axes the gradient is I ÷ V, which is 1 ÷ R. A steeper line therefore means less resistance, not more.
items.random_wrong: both elements are linear, because in each of them the current rises as the pd rises

items.q: In Required practical activity 4 the resistor must be kept at a constant temperature. Why does this matter?
items.correct: so that any change of resistance from heating cannot spoil the results
items.misconception: so that the resistor does not become hot enough to be dangerous to touch
items.why: Temperature effects are invisible in a short experiment, and the wire never feels hot, so the instruction looks like a safety or housekeeping rule. The resistance of a metal wire rises measurably when it warms, so a heating wire would give a resistance-against-length line that bends. Keeping the current small and switching off between readings holds the temperature steady.
items.random_wrong: so that the cell is not drained by the current passing through the wire

items.q: A charge flow of 720 C passes through a component in 3.0 minutes. Calculate the current.
items.correct: 4 A
items.why: The equation is memorised as V = I R, a multiplication, and the multiplication sign is then carried over into every rearrangement of it. Rearranging V = I R gives R = V ÷ I and I = V ÷ R. Only the subject of the original equation is a product; the other two are quotients.

items.q: A current of 0.50 A passes through a 12 Ω resistor. Calculate the potential difference across the resistor.
items.why: The equation is memorised as V = I R, a multiplication, and the multiplication sign is then carried over into every rearrangement of it. Rearranging V = I R gives R = V ÷ I and I = V ÷ R. Only the subject of the original equation is a product; the other two are quotients.

items.q: Which description matches the I–V graph of a filament lamp?
items.correct: an S-shaped curve that flattens as the pd rises
items.misconception: a straight line through the origin, in both directions
items.why: Students take through the origin as the whole test and stop there, or they take rising together to mean directly proportional. A curve that rises does look like agreement with the rule. Directly proportional means a straight line through the origin, so that equal increases in pd give equal increases in current. The lamp's line bends over, so its resistance is not constant.
items.random_wrong: a straight line whose gradient rises with the pd

items.q: A 3.0 Ω resistor and a 6.0 Ω resistor are connected in series. What is the total resistance of the combination?
items.correct: it is 9.0 Ω, because series resistances add together
items.misconception: it is 2.0 Ω, because the charge now divides between two paths
items.why: The series and parallel rules are memorised as two rival formulas without a picture of the circuit. 'Two resistors' cues the more distinctive reciprocal formula, and each extra component is wrongly counted as an extra path for the charge. Count the paths, not the components. In series there is one path: every coulomb must pass through both resistors in turn, so the oppositions accumulate and R_total = R1 + R2 = 9.0 ohm. Only when the resistors sit on separate branches between the same two points does the charge divide, and only then does 1/R = 1/R1 + 1/R2 apply, giving a total smaller than either resistor.
items.random_wrong: it is 6.0 Ω, set by the larger of the two resistors

items.q: A current of 0.40 A flows for 5.0 minutes. What goes into Q = I t?
items.correct: The time must be converted to seconds first: 5.0 minutes is 300 s, so Q = 0.40 × 300 = 120 C.
items.misconception: You mishandle the minutes-to-seconds conversion: substituting the time as given, so Q = 0.40 × 5.0 = 2 C, or using just 60 s, so Q = 0.40 × 60 = 24 C
items.why: The equation does not visibly contain a unit, so students treat t as just a number. In most other calculations the numbers given are used exactly as they are printed. The specification defines time, t, in seconds, s. The equation is only true with that unit, so minutes must be multiplied by 60 and hours by 3600 before substituting.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: What exactly is flowing when there is a current in a wire?
items.correct: Electrical charge. The size of the current is the rate of flow of that charge.
items.misconception: Current is the flow of energy round the circuit, or it is how fast the electrons are moving.
items.why: Circuits are taught alongside energy transfer, so current and energy get merged. And rate of flow does sound like a speed, so the electrons' speed is substituted for the amount of charge passing each second. Current is charge per second, not joules per second and not metres per second. Electrons drift at well under a millimetre per second even when the current is several amperes.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Does potential difference flow through a component?
items.correct: No. Current flows through a component; potential difference is across it, between its two ends.
items.misconception: Potential difference flows through a component in the same way that current does.
items.why: Both quantities are talked about in the same sentence, and everyday talk about electricity flowing covers both words. The voltmeter is also read as measuring something inside the wire. Potential difference is a difference between two points, so it needs two ends to be measured between; that is why a voltmeter is connected across a component and an ammeter in the loop.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Does it matter where in a series loop the ammeter is placed?
items.correct: No. A current has the same value at any point in a single closed loop, so any position in that loop gives the same reading.
items.misconception: An ammeter nearer the cell reads a bigger current than one further round the loop.
items.why: Current is pictured as something poured out by the cell and gradually thinning as it travels, so distance from the cell is expected to matter. Charge cannot pile up or disappear in a wire, so the same number of coulombs passes every point each second. The ammeter can go anywhere in the loop.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Two resistors of different values are connected in series. What is the total resistance?
items.correct: The two resistances add, so the total is their sum and is larger than either resistor on its own.
items.misconception: The total resistance is the average of the two resistance values, so it lies between them.
items.why: Faced with two numbers and unsure how to combine them, students fall back on averaging, the operation they most often use to combine values; it also gives an answer that sits comfortably between the two, which feels reasonable. Resistors in series are joined end to end, so the charge must pass through both and their resistances add. The total is always larger than either one, never a value between them.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: A small and a large resistor are connected in series. What decides the total resistance?
items.correct: Both do: the resistances add, so the total is the sum of the two and is larger than either alone.
items.misconception: The larger resistor sets the total resistance, because it is the main obstacle to the current and the small one hardly matters.
items.why: Students picture the biggest resistor as a bottleneck that governs the whole circuit, by analogy with a chain being only as strong as its weakest link, so the smaller resistor is treated as negligible. In series the charge meets both resistors one after the other, so each adds its full share; the total is the sum, 3.0 Ω + 6.0 Ω = 9.0 Ω, not just the larger value.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: A student wants to measure both the current through a lamp and the potential difference across it. Should both meters be connected across the lamp?
items.correct: No. Only the voltmeter goes across (in parallel with) the lamp. The ammeter must go in the loop, in series with the lamp, so that the current being measured passes through it.
items.misconception: A meter measures a component just by being connected to it, so both the ammeter and the voltmeter are drawn across the lamp, in parallel with it.
items.why: Everyday measuring devices, like a thermometer, are simply put in contact with the thing being measured, and the voltmeter's 'across the component' rule is generalised to all meters. The idea that an ammeter must carry the very current it reads is never formed. An ammeter counts the charge flowing per second, so that flow must pass through it: it goes in series, in the loop with the lamp. A voltmeter compares the potential at the lamp's two terminals, so it goes in parallel, across the lamp. An ammeter placed in parallel would short-circuit the lamp because of its very low resistance.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

specSource: AQA GCSE Physics (8463) specification; section 4.2.1 Current, potential difference and resistance
